articles.title: Pakistani astronaut to join China’s next space station mission
articles.text:
Pakistani astronaut to join China’s next space station mission | Space News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
A woman and two boys gather by a giant figure of an astronaut as they pose for pictures next to the Wulanhada Volcano Geopark visitor centre in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, China, July 26, 2026 [Maxim Shemetov/Reuters]
By Al Jazeera Staff, AFP and Reuters
Published On 7 Nov 20267 Nov 2026
China’s Manned Space Agency has selected a Pakistani astronaut as a payload specialist for its upcoming Shenzhou-24 mission, making the unnamed individual the first foreign national to visit the country’s space station.
The Pakistani astronaut would join China’s Shenzhou-24 mission, as part of bilateral cooperation under Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative, Chinese state media reported on Saturday.
Recommended Stories list of 4 items
list 1 of 4 Which countries have sent people to space?
list 2 of 4 Japan launches historic mission to bring back Mars moon samples
list 3 of 4 Why are US, Russia and China racing to put nuclear reactors on the moon?
list 4 of 4 ‘Alien-cortical’ mice: Can human brain cells grow inside animals?end of list
China has not identified the astronaut nor given a date of departure, but the mission is expected to take place by the end of the year.
Pakistani pilots Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud spent months training at the China Astronaut Research and Training Center in Beijing for a mission.
Last February, Pakistan and China, longstanding strategic and diplomatic partners, entered into an agreement, establishing a Chinese government-led programme to train Pakistani astronauts. China is Pakistan’s largest trading partner and a key foreign investor.
The China National Space Administration will also deploy Jinnah-1, Pakistan’s inaugural lunar rover. Weighing 35kg (77lb) and fitted with specialised scientific equipment, the rover is tasked with analysing plasma behaviour, radiation, and the composition of lunar soil.
The training programme includes practical operational exercises and intensive Chinese language lessons to prepare the candidates for the mission.
Beijing’s China Central Television reported that after completing a short-term in-orbit flight, the astronauts would return to Earth on board the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft.
China invested heavily in its space programme in recent years – catching up with its main rival, the United States – and aims to land astronauts on the Moon by 2030.
Advertisement
The US, Russia, and China are also racing to build nuclear reactors on the Moon. While the US space agency, NASA, announced plans to develop a nuclear reactor on the Moon by the end of 2030, Russia has been working with China and aims to do the same by 2036.
The reactors will be needed to power the mining of frozen water trapped deep in the moon’s craters, which scientists believe could supply drinking water, air, and rocket fuel for future bases. The reactors would also provide power for lunar bases.

articles.title: US Senator Abdul El-Sayed launches ‘Habibi’ political action committee
articles.text:
US Senator Abdul El-Sayed launches ‘Habibi’ political action committee | Politics News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
Democratic Senator Abdul El-Sayed reacts after his victory in the US midterm elections, in Detroit, Michigan, United States [File: Brian Snyder/Reuters]
By Al Jazeera Staff
Published On 7 Nov 20267 Nov 2026
Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed has launched a political action committee called “Habibi PAC”, days after becoming the first Muslim member of the United States Senate.
Political action committees, or PACs, are organisations that raise and spend money to support or oppose candidates for office.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 ‘Call me senator’: How Abdul El-Sayed beat Trump’s hate to create history
list 2 of 3 The biggest winners and losers of the 2026 US midterms
list 3 of 3 Abdul El-Sayed did not have to become less Muslim to winend of list
A Federal Election Commission filing dated on Thursday shows that Habibi PAC is registered as a leadership PAC sponsored by El-Sayed. Such committees are separate from a politician’s own campaign.
Habibi, an Arabic term of endearment meaning “my dear” or “my beloved”, is a word El-Sayed used often on the campaign trail, including in his victory speech in Detroit, when he addressed Vice President JD Vance directly: “JD, habibi, there is this delicious irony in the fact that you’re constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January.”
He is one of several newly elected Democrats to register leadership PACs since Tuesday’s vote, according to FEC filings. They include Arizona Congressman-elect Amish Shah’s “PACStreet Boy”, Iowa Senator-elect Josh Turek’s “WheelPAC” and North Carolina Senator-elect Roy Cooper’s “One NC PAC”.
According to OpenSecrets, ambitious lawmakers use leadership PACs to gain clout with colleagues and strengthen bids for leadership posts or committee chairmanships by giving to other members, their party and other political committees.
In the 2024 election cycle, leadership PACs gave $79.3m to federal candidates. Most went to Republicans, although a Democratic leadership PAC was the biggest single donor.
Advertisement
El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, defeated Republican Mike Rogers after a campaign in which Trump, Vance and Senator Ted Cruz questioned his loyalty, called him a “jihadist” and attempted to link him to the Muslim Brotherhood movement, without providing any evidence.
Speaking to Al Jazeera at a rally in the Michigan city of Wyandotte days before the vote, El-Sayed said taxpayers’ money should be spent saving lives at home rather than going to foreign governments committing genocide or apartheid.
He added that defeating Trump was not enough and that the system that produced him had to be replaced.
Getting money out of politics was one of his central pledges. In his victory speech, he said the result showed that in a battle between money and the many, “the many can win”.
His win came amid the most expensive midterm election on record. According to an analysis of FEC data by OpenSecrets, total spending is expected to reach $11.9bn, up from $8.9bn in 2022.
Outside spending, driven by super PACs, is projected to hit $3.9bn, an 85 percent increase on 2022. So-called dark money from undisclosed donors has already reached at least $1.47bn, surpassing the 2024 record of $1.35bn, which included the presidential race.
OpenSecrets found that conservative groups outspent liberal ones on outside spending by about $360m, while Democratic candidates were expected to outspend Republican candidates by roughly $800m.

articles.title: Houston mayor curbs cooperation of US city’s police with ICE
articles.text:
Houston mayor curbs cooperation of US city’s police with ICE | US Midterm Elections 2026 News | Al Jazeera
US Midterm Elections 2026
Save
Share
Houston Mayor John Whitmire [File: Kirby Lee/US Today Sports]
By Al Jazeera Staff and Reuters
Published On 7 Nov 20267 Nov 2026
The mayor of Houston, the most populous city in the US state of Texas, has ordered the city’s police force to sharply limit its cooperation with the United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
John Whitmire’s executive order came on Friday, days after Democrats swept statewide offices in the traditionally Republican state.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 Can America ever return to pre-Trump politics?
list 2 of 3 Republicans redrew this Texas district to win – it narrowly worked
list 3 of 3 How the US midterm elections reflected resistance to data centresend of list
According to the order, Houston police will contact ICE only when a person is being arrested for a jailable offence, according to the Reuters news agency.
Whitmire said he had consulted Texas’s newly elected governor, lieutenant governor and comptroller before acting, and that the move was meant to reduce fear and anxiety across the city.
“Elections matter,” Whitmire told reporters. “I do this to begin a healing process,” he said, adding he hoped his executive order would become a model for other Texas cities.
Joining Whitmire at the news conference, Houston Police ⁠Chief J Noe Diaz said he supported the change and that his department had already begun to implement the new policy.
Under the new rules, people stopped for minor traffic violations will no longer be referred to ICE simply because they have an administrative immigration warrant.
The decision reverses a policy Whitmire put in place in April under pressure from outgoing Republican Governor Greg Abbott.
Abbott had threatened to withdraw about $110m in state public safety grants, arguing that a city council ordinance limiting police contact with ICE breached Senate Bill 4, a 2017 state law that bars local police from restricting cooperation with federal immigration authorities.
Advertisement
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton also sued the mayor, the city council and the police chief over the ordinance.
“We’re taking an interpretation of the law today, working with the newly elected members of the state leadership, in implementing this policy,” Whitmire told reporters. “We don’t want people to worry about ⁠their workers, their family members, their students.”
The issue has drawn intense scrutiny in Houston. The Houston Chronicle found that city police contacted ICE at least 107 times in the first eight months of 2025, compared with nine times in the whole of 2024.
In July, an ICE agent shot dead Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a longtime Houston resident.
FIEL Houston, an immigrant rights group, called the order a victory for the city but said it was long overdue. “Today Houston won. Today our community can breathe easier,” FIEL Executive Director Cesar Espinosa said in a statement to KPRC.
Whitmire said he expected Houston’s approach to become a model for other cities. In Austin, Mayor Kirk Watson asked city officials on Friday to revise their own policy on ICE warrants.

articles.title: Two main parties neck and neck after New Zealand vote, early results
articles.text:
Two main parties neck and neck after New Zealand vote, early results | Elections News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
Supporters cheer at the election party of Christopher Luxon, leader of the National Party, in Auckland, New Zealand, on November 7, 2026 [David Rowland/Reuters]
By Al Jazeera Staff and Reuters
Published On 7 Nov 20267 Nov 2026
New Zealand’s governing centre-right National Party and main opposition Labour have both secured just short of 30 percent of the popular vote, with more than 80 percent of the election results counted.
The Electoral Commission on Saturday showed the current three-party ruling coalition led by National would have a majority of just one seat, after an election dominated by a struggling economy and voter disillusionment with the two biggest contenders.
It added that the centrist Opportunity Party will meet the 5 percent threshold to enter parliament, potentially becoming a kingmaker.
Polling stations opened at 9am on Saturday (20:00 GMT Friday) and closed at 7pm (06:00 GMT Saturday).
New Zealand’s Electoral Commission aims to release preliminary results from 95 percent of polling stations by the end of election night on Saturday. A final result, which will reflect ballots cast by New Zealanders abroad, is expected by November 27.
There is no timeframe for when a government must be formed.
New Zealand’s opposition leader Chris Hipkins said the country’s politicians would need to find “common ground”, as results showed neither main party was likely to win an overall majority.
“New Zealand has spoken. It may take us a little bit longer to figure out exactly what it is that you’ve said,” Hipkins told supporters. “Our next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together, and to find common ground.”
Supporters gather at Labour Party leader Chris Hipkins’s election night watch party, in Upper Hutt, New Zealand, on November 7, 2026 [Hollie Adams/Reuters]
New Zealand’s 2026 election has been at times dubbed the “supermarket election”, where grocery prices and supermarket competition have become a key battleground for political parties.
Advertisement
Peter Dunne, a former member of New Zealand’s parliament, who also served as a minister in both National and Labour-led governments, said that the election is “much more of a cost-of-living election”, with voters essentially looking at “which of the main blocs is better placed to ease the cost of living burden on New Zealanders”.
“The ruling coalition appears well ahead of the centre-left. Now, that may change because these are early results, but it’s a little bit of a surprise that this is happening,” Dunne told Al Jazeera. “We were looking to a much tighter contest than appears to be the case at the moment.”
The National Party pledged to return the budget to surplus through fiscal discipline while expanding the national pension scheme. The Labour Party promised cheaper healthcare and transport.
The former minister added that both main parties are practically “carbon copies of the other”, leaving “a whole rising generation of voters, who want to see a bit more adventure in politics”.
Dunne said that, therefore, the results show support rallying behind other parties, like “strong support for the Green Party, the right-wing libertarian [ACT New Zealand], the xenophobic nationalist [New Zealand First] party, and a new centrist party, the Opportunity Party, which wants to be in the middle between all of them”.
He told Al Jazeera that even though the Opportunity Party is currently hovering around 5 percent at the moment – also the threshold for representation in parliament – “it’s been one of the big stars of this campaign”.
Political party billboards in a suburb of Wellington, New Zealand, on October 31, 2026 [Charlotte Graham-McLay/AP]
New Zealand holds a general election every three years under a mixed-member proportional system.
Voters do not elect a leader of the country, but instead select a local electorate candidate and a political party.
Dunne told Al Jazeera that if both main parties of the blocs “end up relatively evenly placed, then the onus could go on the Opportunity Party”.
“If Opportunity Party reaches parliament, it will talk to the largest party first, which appears to be the National Party, but there’s no guarantee that they could come to an arrangement,” he said.
“We could face weeks of interparty negotiations to form a government. Parliament has to sit by early January, so there’s a real prospect that we could go into Christmas with no clear government in New Zealand,” Dunne added.
Electorate winners earn a seat in the typically 120-seat parliament, as do the highest-ranked members of the party, based on their national party vote.
Advertisement
All votes are counted by hand, not by machine.
Advertisement

articles.title: Russia launches missile attack on Kyiv, injuring residents
articles.text:
Russia launches missile attack on Kyiv, injuring residents | Russia-Ukraine war News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
A residential building lies in ruins after a Russian air strike on Komyshuvakha, in Ukraine’s Zaporizhia region [Evgeniy Maloletka/AP Photo]
By Al Jazeera Staff, AP and Reuters
Published On 7 Nov 20267 Nov 2026
Russian forces have launched a missile attack on the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv’s mayor said, after President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned in his nightly video address that Russia was preparing new attacks on energy targets, bridges and other infrastructure.
Debris from Saturday’s attack damaged a residential building, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Recommended Stories list of 4 items
list 1 of 4 Russia to UAE, Iran steps up diplomacy amid Trump threats: What we know
list 2 of 4 Ukraine raises Zaporizhia aid strike death toll to at least 50
list 3 of 4 What a Trump-Xi-Putin summit could mean – and what it wouldn’t
list 4 of 4 Russia’s land gains in Ukraine dwindle as its diesel ‘goes unsold’end of list
“Explosions in the Kyiv suburbs. The enemy is hitting infrastructure with ballistic missiles,” Klitschko wrote on Telegram.
Klitschko said debris had struck a five-storey apartment building in a western district of the capital. The facade of another residential building was also damaged.
The city’s military administration said on Telegram that two people were injured and a building housing a kindergarten was damaged.
Officials continued to warn residents of the potential for more strikes hours after the attack.
The attacks come as Zelenskyy said his government is seeking specific guarantees from Western allies on how post-war security support would function. He made comments in an interview aired late on Thursday, following two days of discussions among allies in Brussels.
The talks in Brussels discussed post-war reconstruction, funding for next year and security guarantees backed by the Ukrainian government’s Western allies.
The meetings brought together officials from the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Germany and the European Union, along with representatives from the World Bank and the US investment group BlackRock, Ukrainian lead negotiator Rustem Umerov wrote in an online post.
US-led talks
The attacks occurred three days before US-led Ukrainian-Russian talks were to open in Abu Dhabi seeking a resolution to the war that has gone on for more than four years. The last such talks took place in February.
Advertisement
On Thursday, US President Donald Trump said a deal between Russia and Ukraine may be imminent, following a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s special envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, at the White House.
Trump said he did not meet the Ukrainian delegation on Thursday.
The meeting between the US president and Dmitriev came on the same day as First Lady Melania Trump hosted a diplomatic gathering with Russian and Ukrainian representatives to mark and build on a localised truce she helped broker in the southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky in October.
The truce expired last Sunday, a day before a Russian bombing of an aid distribution point in Komyshuvakha, in the Zaporizhia region.
The death toll from the attack has risen to 50, Ukraine’s Emergency Service said on Friday, making it one of the ⁠deadliest strikes on ⁠civilians this year.
Advertisement

articles.title: How the US midterm elections reflected resistance to data centres
articles.text:
How the US midterm elections reflected resistance to data centres | US Midterm Elections 2026 News | Al Jazeera
US Midterm Elections 2026
Save
Share
Democrats sought to leverage public backlash against data centres during the midterm elections [Nathan Howard/Reuters]
By Andy Hirschfeld
Published On 7 Nov 20267 Nov 2026
In September, a poll found that 70 percent of Democrats and 57 percent of Republicans supported limiting the construction of new data centres in the United States.
But that opposition was tested in Tuesday’s midterm election, with analysts examining key races to see if the public backlash would translate into votes.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 Global tech stocks plunge over fears of AI curbs in US
list 2 of 3 Tech stock rout, driven by US AI fears, continues in Asian trading
list 3 of 3 Protesters break into Microsoft AI data centre site in Amsterdamend of list
It did. There were 41 ballot measures related to data centres in Tuesday’s midterms, spread across the country.
According to Data Centers on the Ballot, an election-monitoring project run by Redbud Consulting, voters are on track to reject data centre development in all but one of the contests.
Two of the races continue to be counted but are expected to result in majorities to reject or limit data centres.
Only Harwood, North Dakota, a small town with a population of fewer than 800 people, voted to oppose such limits. The measure it defeated would have required independent reviews of large industrial projects like data centres before they could be built in the area.
Experts say Tuesday’s midterm elections indicate that the debate around data centres has become a bipartisan issue, intertwined with cost-of-living concerns and fears over job stability.
A construction boom
As of April, the Pew Research Center estimated that there were already 3,000 data centres in the country, with more than 1,500 others in progress.
The construction boom has been driven in large part by the growth in the artificial intelligence (AI) sector. That industry, experts say, has fed concerns about a shifting economic landscape.
Advertisement
“The unchecked acceleration of AI development has been causing concern across the board,” Bhaskar Chakravorti, the dean of global business at Tufts University, told Al Jazeera.
“People worry about their jobs and what it might mean from a broader economic perspective. But closer to home, people could see the physical manifestations of AI in data centres being built in their back yards, or they were hearing about it from others.”
Not only are voters afraid that AI might replace human work, but they also fear the downstream costs of data centres, according to Chakravorti.
Data centres consume large amounts of water and energy, which critics say can drive up electricity costs for nearby communities.
“Whether higher energy costs were driven by broader factors, such as the Iran war or tariffs, AI competing for space on the electricity grid was certainly part of its unpopularity,” Chakravorti said.
Voters, he added, were seeing the results “in their energy bills”.
A 2026 working paper from the Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas estimated that, as of last year, wholesale electricity prices had risen by 6.9 percent as a result of data centres.
James Mercer, founder of Metro Colo Advisory, an independent data centre advisory firm, told Al Jazeera that those anticipated costs mobilised voters in many areas.
“What they push back on is a building down the road that needs as much power as a small city, when they suspect their own electric bill will cover it,” Mercer said.
“That’s why local resistance has grown so fast: counties pausing new projects, zoning fights and data centres turning into a ballot issue.”
An election-season talking point
That popular resistance led several candidates in high-profile races to make AI and data-centre development central to their campaigns.
Among them is Democrat Sherrod Brown, who flipped a key Senate seat in Ohio, the state that accounted for the largest share of data-centre ballot initiatives this year.
Some 21 votes were taken on data centres in the state, out of a total of 47 referendums and measures that took place across the country in 2026.
Brown, a former senator, made Republican incumbent Jon Husted’s support for data-centre development a key point of attack.
“One guy has led the charge on these. That guy’s responsible, and that’s Jon Husted,” Brown told NBC News earlier this year.
In Texas, meanwhile, Democrat Gina Hinojosa called for a moratorium on new data-centre approvals until stronger protections for local communities were put in place.
Though her position worried tech investors keen on expansion in the Lone Star State, Hinojosa ultimately defeated incumbent Greg Abbott in the governor’s race.
Advertisement
“While Abbott had a moratorium on data centres in Texas currently, the overriding view is this would end once he got re-elected,” Dan Ives, managing director at the bank Yorkville Ives, said in an analyst note.
“Hinojosa is a known anti-data center politician and negative on the AI buildout, which makes worries around the future of the data center buildout in Texas a real issue for tech investors.”
Another successful Democratic candidate, Senator-elect James Talarico, also flipped a Republican-held seat with a pledge to increase data centre regulation.
Texas has been at the centre of growing concerns over the water demands of AI infrastructure.
The city of Corpus Christi, for example, has faced severe drought conditions, with its reservoir falling to just 8 percent of its total capacity earlier this year.
The city has been described as at risk of running out of drinking water. Talarico proposed adopting closed-loop water systems to reduce data centre consumption. He also advocated for data centre operators to fund local infrastructure improvements.
He won Corpus Christi by a 12-percentage-point margin.

articles.title: ‘One less gang leader’: Haiti’s prime minister celebrates police operation
articles.text:
‘One less gang leader’: Haiti’s prime minister celebrates police operation | Crime News | Al Jazeera
Save
Share
Haiti Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aime speaks to journalists in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, on November 3 [Patrice Noel/Reuters]
By Al Jazeera Staff
Published On 7 Nov 20267 Nov 2026
Haiti’s National Police (PNH) has confirmed that a gang leader known as Mathias Saintil was “neutralised” as part of a recent law enforcement operation.
In a social media post shared on Friday, officials described Saintil as the leader of the Boston gang, named for a neighbourhood in Cite Soleil, an impoverished part of the capital, Port-au-Prince.
Recommended Stories list of 3 items
list 1 of 3 El Salvador’s Bukele threatens Haitian gangs over abducted soldiers
list 2 of 3 El Salvador pledges more than 2,000 soldiers as Haiti delays elections
list 3 of 3 El Salvador’s Bukele touts military intervention in Haitiend of list
Saintil was reportedly struck by “multiple bullets” during a law enforcement operation, and a police source said he died later in the hospital.
Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aime celebrated the news with a social media post of his own.
“One less gang leader,” he wrote in a mix of French and Haitian Creole. “The battle to liberate the country from the grip of bandits continues with determination. The gangs won’t be able to sleep!”
Haiti has struggled with a surge in gang violence for years, most notably after the assassination of then-President Jovenel Moise in 2021.
The assassination left the country in crisis, and no national elections have been held in the years since. Amid the political turmoil, organised crime in Haiti sought to expand its influence, claiming large swaths of territory.
As much as 90 percent of Port-au-Prince has fallen under gang control, including key roadways and maritime ports. At least 26 gangs operate in the area in and around the capital, according to the United Nations.
Haiti has long struggled with political instability, economic decline and successive natural disasters. It has been ranked as the poorest country in the Western Hemisphere.
Advertisement
The country’s gangs often recruit young people with the promise of food, income and protection. The UN estimates that half of the country’s gang members are children and teens under the age of 18.
The violence, however, has led to a spiralling humanitarian crisis. At least 1.4 million people have been displaced from their homes, particularly in the capital area.
Some 1,123 Haitians were killed in the violence between July and October of this year, according to the UN. Another 440 people were injured during that time period, and rates of sexual violence remain high: Between July and August, there were 689 cases of gang-involved rape.
The crisis has prompted widespread outcry. In April, members of a new international Gang Suppression Force (GSF) began arriving in Haiti, with a mission to “neutralise, isolate and deter gangs”.
Its 12-month mandate was renewed in September, with the UN Security Council granting an extension until March 2027.
But the GSF has encountered many of the same setbacks that faced its predecessor, the Kenyan-led Multinational Security Support (MSS) — namely, insufficient resources and staffing.
Proponents of the GSF have called on the international community to fulfil its commitments by funding the force to the fullest extent.
Members of the GSF have also come under attack as part of their clashes with Haiti’s gangs. On October 18, for instance, four Salvadoran aviation technicians involved in the GSF were kidnapped.
El Salvador has responded by surging as many as 2,000 troops to Haiti. Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele described the deployment as a rescue mission.
“We have one single objective: to ensure our four compatriots return home alive and unharmed,” Bukele wrote on October 21, sharing a video of armoured vehicles patrolling Haitian streets, some firing guns.
“But I want you — the gang leaders — to understand one thing very clearly,” Bukele added. “Today’s attack is nothing compared to what is coming if you do not return all four hostages alive.”
He has since called on Haitians to “rise up” and “reclaim control of your communities”. He also insisted that his forces are not “invaders”.
Human rights watchdogs have criticised Bukele for his heavy-handed approach to gang violence in El Salvador, which he has addressed in part through mass arrests and mass trials.
Bukele has warned he is “capable” of deploying the same tactics against Haiti’s gangs. In his latest post on Friday, Bukele interacted with a social media user who suggested they had identified the residence of a prominent Haitian gang leader.
Advertisement
“Where is this house located?” Bukele asked. “Give us the exact address, and we will destroy it.”
Advertisement
